original_value: The combination of the explosive growth in digital data and the demand to preserve much of these data in the long term has made it imperative to find a more cost-effective way than HDD arrays and a more easily accessible way than tape libraries to store massive amounts of data. While modern optical discs are capable of guaranteeing more than 50-year data preservation without media replacement, individual optical discs’ lack of the performance and capacity relative to HDDs or tapes has significantly limited their use in datacenters. This article presents a Rack-scale Optical disc library System, or ROS in short, which provides a PB-level total capacity and inline accessibility on thousands of optical discs built within a 42U Rack. A rotatable roller and robotic arm separating and fetching discs are designed to improve disc placement density and simplify the mechanical structure. A hierarchical storage system based on SSDs, hard disks, and optical discs is proposed to effectively hide the delay of mechanical operation. However, an optical library file system (OLFS) based on FUSE is proposed to schedule mechanical operation and organize data on the tiered storage with a POSIX user interface to provide an illusion of inline data accessibility. We further optimize OLFS by reducing unnecessary user/kernel context switches inheriting from legacy FUSE framework. We evaluate ROS on a few key performance metrics, including operation delays of the mechanical structure and software overhead in a prototype PB-level ROS system. The results show that ROS stacked on Samba and FUSE as network-attached storage (NAS) mode almost saturates the throughput provided by underlying samba via 10GbE network for external users, as well as in this scenario provides about 53ms file write and 15ms read latency, exhibiting its inline accessibility. Besides, ROS is able to effectively hide and virtualize internal complex operational behaviors and be easily deployable in datacenters.

result.paraphrase: Exploding digital-data growth and the need for long-term preservation have created a need for a storage approach that is more economical than HDD arrays and more accessible than tape libraries for massive datasets. Although modern optical discs can preserve data for over 50 years without media replacement, their limited performance and capacity compared with HDDs or tapes have constrained adoption in datacenters. This article introduces a Rack-scale Optical disc library System (ROS), which delivers PB-level aggregate capacity and inline access across thousands of optical discs housed in a 42U rack. To increase disc-placement density and simplify the mechanical design, it uses a rotatable roller and a robotic arm for separating and retrieving discs. A hierarchical storage architecture built from SSDs, hard disks, and optical discs is proposed to mask the delay of mechanical operations. In addition, an optical library file system (OLFS) based on FUSE is proposed to schedule those operations and organize tiered data through a POSIX user interface, creating the illusion of inline data accessibility. OLFS is further optimized by cutting unnecessary user/kernel context switches inherited from the legacy FUSE framework. ROS is evaluated on several key performance metrics, including mechanical-operation delays and software overhead in a prototype PB-scale system. Results show that ROS, stacked on Samba and FUSE in NAS mode, nearly saturates the throughput of the underlying Samba over a 10GbE network for external users; in this setting it also delivers about 53 ms write latency and 15 ms read latency, demonstrating inline accessibility. In addition, ROS effectively hides and virtualizes complex internal operations and is easy to deploy in datacenters.
